claims.text: Equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo is a disordered BCC alloy.
Equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo has a room-temperature compressive yield strength of 1719 MPa.
The baseline alloy has limited room-temperature plasticity.
Substituting part of the Mo with V will reduce the alloy's overall electronegativity difference.
V has a lower electronegativity than Mo.
Small-to-moderate V-for-Mo substitution will preserve the disordered BCC structure.
V substitution will moderate charge-density differences and lattice strain caused by the high Mo content.
Reduced electronegativity difference will decrease localized bonding heterogeneity.
Decreased localized bonding heterogeneity will facilitate dislocation motion.
Easier dislocation motion will increase room-temperature compressive plastic strain.
Solid-solution strengthening associated with the disordered BCC structure will preserve most of the alloy's yield strength after V substitution.
The modified alloy will retain a room-temperature compressive yield strength above approximately 1650 MPa.
The modified alloy will show a noticeable increase in room-temperature compressive plastic strain relative to equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo.
The beneficial strength-plasticity effect should be limited to V substitutions of no more than roughly 20% of the Mo.
V substitutions beyond roughly 20% of the Mo may cause phase instability or loss of the high-strength disordered BCC microstructure.
Processing conditions can alter the extent of chemical short-range order and lattice distortion.

contradictions.description: The phrase '10 at% of Mo' is compositionally ambiguous: the stated NbZrTiHfMo0.9V0.1 formula corresponds after normalization to 2 at% V and 18 at% Mo, whereas '10 at%' could be read as 10 atomic-percentage points of the whole alloy. The substitution series likewise does not specify whether its percentages are fractions of Mo sites or total-alloy atomic percentages.

The predicted retained-strength criterion is above 1650 MPa, but the falsification rule only treats strength below 1500 MPa as a significant loss. Thus, an alloy yielding between 1500 and 1650 MPa while improving plasticity would violate the quantified prediction without falsifying the hypothesis under the stated rule.
